segments.say: Let's move gently through the body now. Not to fix anything, or to check anything, but simply to visit, the way you might walk slowly through a quiet house at night, switching off the last few lamps. Wherever the day still lingers, we'll pause for a moment, and let it soften.

Remember, earlier tonight, how Walter Cannon described the body getting ready for action. The heart speeding up, the muscles tightening, everything prepared to push or to run. That was useful, once, on a hot bus with a sharp message on the screen. But there's no action needed now. The body is allowed to stand down.

show.text: No action needed now. The body is allowed to stand down.

segments.say: Start with your forehead. Notice if there's any tightness there, any small frown left over from the day. You don't need to force it away. Just imagine the skin above your eyes becoming smooth and wide, like a sheet being gently shaken out and laid flat on a bed.

Now your eyes. If they're closed, let them be closed softly, without squeezing. Let the little muscles around them loosen. Let your eyelids feel heavy, warm, a little sleepy. There's nothing you need to see right now. Let them rest in the dark.

Forehead, softening. Eyes, heavy and still. Cheeks, relaxed. And now, the jaw, which is where a lot of anger likes to hide. We'll stay there for a little while. There's no hurry. The face has been busy all day, frowning and smiling, talking and listening, reacting to everything around it. Now it has nothing left to react to. Only the quiet of the room.

So many of us clench our jaws without knowing it. In traffic, in queues, reading a message that stings. The teeth press together, the muscles near the ears go tight. Let that go now. Let your teeth part, just a little. Let your tongue rest softly in your mouth. Let the jaw hang loose and easy.

Breathe in. And as you breathe out, let the jaw loosen just a little more. You might be surprised how much more it can let go. It's been working hard all day, holding things in, biting things back. It can rest now. There's nothing left to say tonight.

Let your lips rest lightly together, or part a little, whichever is more comfortable. Let the corners of your mouth soften. Maybe the hint of a small smile, if it comes on its own, but there's no need to make one. Just a soft, easy line, the way a face looks when it's finally, truly at rest.

Now let's move down to the hands. Picture a pair of soft gloves lying open on a bench, empty and relaxed, nothing to hold. Your hands can be like that now. Open. Loose. Resting wherever they've landed. They don't need to grip a phone, or a bag, or a handrail tonight.

Earlier today, perhaps, your hands closed into tight shapes without you noticing. Around a phone, around a strap on the bus, around the edge of a table. Let the fingers uncurl now, one by one. Let the palms soften. Feel the warmth flowing into them, all the way to the fingertips.
Open hands have nothing to hold on to. No grudges, no sharp replies, no clenched fists. Just warmth, and stillness, and rest. Let them stay open like that, for as long as you like.

show.text: Open hands have nothing to hold on to.

segments.say: Now your shoulders. Notice where they are. So often, at the end of a long day, they've crept up towards the ears without us realising, carrying the weight of everything. Let them drop now. Let them sink down, away from your ears, heavier and heavier, as if someone kind had lifted a heavy coat from your back.

And as the shoulders drop, let the neck lengthen and soften. Let your head rest its full weight on the pillow. You don't need to hold it up anymore. The pillow is doing all the work. Your neck can simply let go, and rest.

Feel your arms growing heavier now, from the shoulders, down past the elbows, down to the wrists and hands. Warm and heavy, sinking a little into the bed. There's nothing they need to do. No reaching, no lifting, no carrying. Just resting.

Shoulders, low and soft. Neck, long and loose. Arms, heavy and warm. Hands, open and still. Everything the day asked of them, finished now. All the carrying and holding and reaching, all the small efforts you made without noticing, they're done. Nothing more is needed from your shoulders, or your arms, or your hands tonight. They can simply rest, heavy and warm, until morning comes.

Now let your attention drift down to your chest. This is where we often feel anger first, a kind of heat or pressure, a tightness that rises up and wants to come out. Let's visit it gently now, and see how it feels tonight.

Somewhere inside your chest, your heart is beating. Earlier, maybe, it was fast, ready for something. Now it can slow down. Steady, calm, unhurried. It doesn't need to prepare for anything. It can simply keep its quiet rhythm, the way it does every night while you sleep.

Feel the chest rising gently with each in-breath, and falling with each out-breath. Like a small boat on a calm sea, lifting and settling, lifting and settling. Let any leftover tightness there melt a little with every breath out, like snow melting slowly in the first warm sun.

The heat of the day can cool now. Whatever rose up in you today, whatever pressed against your ribs and wanted to get out, it can settle now. It was only ever information. And you've heard it. It doesn't need to shout anymore.

show.text: The heat of the day can cool now.

segments.say: Now let your attention drift down to your belly. Let it be soft. You don't need to hold it in. Let it rise and fall naturally with your breath, slow and easy. Perhaps it feels warm and full, if you've eaten well tonight. Perhaps it's simply resting. Either way, let it be.

And now your legs. Your hips, your thighs, your knees, your calves, all growing heavier, sinking down into the bed. Let them be completely still. They've carried you through the whole day, up stairs, along pavements, onto buses and off again. They can rest now.

And finally your feet. Let your toes uncurl and spread a little. Let your ankles loosen. Feel the warmth reaching all the way down, to the very soles of your feet. From the top of your head to the tips of your toes, every part of you, resting.

Your head, still. Your hands, open. Your heart, slow. Your feet, warm. All of you, resting, in this quiet room, on this quiet night. The places where the day lingered have been visited, one by one, and each one has softened a little. You don't need to check whether it worked. The body knows what to do with rest. It's been waiting for it all day long.

In a moment, we'll think, very gently, about the part of you that gets angry, and how to be kind to it. But only if you're still awake. If you're drifting off already, let yourself go. That's the best ending of all.
